John Moses and Joseph Kirkland (eds.), History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895). Read here for the town before 1836: the immigration chapter 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age' at printed pages 78-79 and 87-101, the early taverns and hotels at pages 560-561, the 'Real Estate and Insurance' chapter at pages 541-542, the packing trade at page 389, the fire department at pages 207-208, the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy quoted from Blanchard at page 35, and the Biographical sketches of P. F. W. Peck, Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Alexander N. Fullerton at pages 570-577 and 584; and, for the shore of 1812 (T-0471), the chapter 'The Massacre' at pages 49-50, 54 and 60-61 - the low, discontinuous sand-hills south of Twelfth Street, the scattered cottonwoods on the bank's lower reaches, and the two 'Massacre trees' of Eighteenth Street with Mrs. Kinzie's word that they were saplings in 1812.

transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.
transcribes.work: Rufus Blanchard, Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (Wheaton, Ill.: R. Blanchard & Co., 1881)

what_it_does_not_supply: MOST OF WHAT IT WAS FETCHED FOR. Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this work, thirteen earned a claim, twenty-one appear only outside the pre-1836 window, eight appear early and say nothing usable, one (`black`) is only ever the adjective, four are unresolved because the volume carries a surname one character from the index card's spelling, and two are absent outright. The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.
what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.

endings.text: You will answer the Democrat's notice for an apprentice to the printing business. It was printed on 20 May, six weeks ago, so the place may be filled. Ask anyway, and ask early.

You will take your tin and copper to Jones, King & Co., whose notice of 17 June wanted both trades immediately. A fortnight is long enough for someone to have answered first, so go before breakfast is cold.
No notice you read asked for a strong back. The papers advertise trades; carrying is found on the wharf and asked for in person. Tomorrow, try the river first.
You carry a chit for a day's carrying when a vessel next unloads at the forwarding house, with no wage written on it. Be on the wharf when a sail comes in.
You asked to be remembered when there is packing to do. That is a winter promise, with no wage, no name and no date: something to hold on to until December, when the hogs come in.
No work today, but a plan for tomorrow: two notices that asked for trades, a yard waiting on the winter, and a firm that forwards freight by the boatload. A day's work is in prospect.

evidence.text: A notice dated Chicago, 8 June 1835 says the steamboat Michigan will leave Chicago for Detroit and Buffalo, and that for freight or passage one may apply to the master on board or to Newberry & Dole.

evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record newberry_dole_warehouse, whose position is reconstructed and whose note carries both readings without settling them. The stop says the bank is disputed and claims no front door.
evidence.text: Where Newberry & Dole’s forwarding house stood is disputed: one dossier reads the south bank on South Water Street, Andreas puts the firm’s warehouse on the north bank east of the later Rush Street bridge. The scene places it on the south bank as a reconstruction, so the stop claims the firm, not the spot.
Andreas dates George W. Dole’s warehouse and slaughter yard to 1832 and places them close to the later site of the Tremont House, at Lake and Dearborn streets.

evidence.reasoning: Andreas’s packing chapter dates Dole’s 1832 killing to the cold months (hogs in December; the passage is summarised in docs/research/08-fauna.md § 5.2) and the South Branch slaughter-house to 1834 (scan p. 1151); the structure record dole_warehouse_south doubts the yard’s use at the scene date for the same reason. So the stop says the yard has nothing to pack in July rather than staging any work there.
evidence.text: Dole’s packing was winter work, and by July 1835 the killing had probably left this yard: Andreas records hogs packed in December 1832 and a slaughter-house Newberry & Dole built on the South Branch in 1834.

evidence.text: Mark Beaubien built a new house on the north-west corner of Wells and Lake streets; in August 1834 Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of it as a hotel, christened it the Exchange Coffee House, and remained until 1836.

evidence.reasoning: Uses the existing structure records’ scene-date phases and positions. The notices are read from the papers, not from the places; the stops speak of what each firm did and when, not of anyone met at the door.
evidence.text: The four places are exterior stops in the 1 July 1835 scene. The Democrat’s corner is visited as its former office, Newberry & Dole’s house is a reconstructed placement, and no interior, front door, clerk, keeper or vessel in port on the morning is claimed.

The visitor’s search for work, the choice of skill, the asking at the two warehouses, the chit for a day’s carrying, the request to be remembered for the packing, breakfast at the Exchange, the plan for tomorrow, the endings, the timing inputs and the A Day’s Work in Prospect keepsake are invented connective narrative. No firm is claimed to have offered work or named a wage.

opening.text:
JAUNT: WORK ON THE WATERFRONT. Morning, and you need a job. The good news: Chicago in 1835 needs everybody. Buildings go up as fast as lumber comes in, every boat needs unloading, and the papers carry notices headed 'Wanted, immediately'. The bad news: the strangers keep coming 'by land and by water', and half of them want work too.

Choose what you can do, read the notices, ask at two of Newberry & Dole's houses, and plan your next move over breakfast.

premise: Read the town's notices for working hands, ask after work at two Newberry & Dole warehouses and leave with a work chit or a sensible next lead.

choices.consequence: You can set type and pull a press.
choices.label: Type and press

choices.consequence: You can lift, carry and load.
choices.label: A strong back

stops.narrative: Choose the skill you are offering.
stops.text: John Calhoun's Democrat, printed here at first and since May over Jones & King's hardware, wants 'an apprentice at this office to the printing business'. On 17 June Jones, King & Co. printed: 'Wanted, immediately, one copper smith, and one tin and sheet iron worker.' A town building this fast needs printers for its notices and tinsmiths for its stovepipes: since 1833 every stovepipe through a roof must be 'guarded by tin or sheet iron', or the owner pays $5.

choices.consequence: A promise to ask again when there is packing to do.
choices.label: Ask to be remembered for the packing

choices.consequence: There is nothing to ask here in July.
choices.label: Go on to the river

stops.narrative: Ask to be remembered, or go on to the river?
stops.text: Andreas puts George Dole's 1832 warehouse and slaughter yard near Lake and Dearborn. Dole began the town's packing trade here, 'the nucleus of one of those immense industries' that made Chicago famous. But packing is winter work, hogs killed in December, and by 1834 the partners had moved their killing to the South Branch. In July there is nothing to pack.

choices.consequence: A chit: a day's carrying when a vessel next unloads. No wage is written on it.
choices.label: Offer a day's carrying

choices.consequence: You note how goods come off the water, and move on.
choices.label: Watch the wharf and ask nothing

stops.narrative: Ask about work, or watch the wharf?
stops.text: Newberry & Dole have advertised as forwarding and commission merchants since November 1833; in June the American named them agents for the steamboat Michigan to Detroit and Buffalo. When the schooner Illinois came up through the new harbour cut in July 1834, she was cheered at their wharf. Every vessel since has needed hands to unload her, and nobody advertises for those.

choices.consequence: You will apply where a notice asked for hands.
choices.label: Answer a printed notice

choices.consequence: You will be at the river when a sail comes in.
choices.label: Wait on the wharf for a vessel

choices.consequence: You will try the stores and yards in person.
choices.label: Keep asking around town

stops.narrative: Where will you ask first tomorrow?
stops.text: Breakfast at the Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells, built by Mark Beaubien and kept by the Murphys since August 1834. The county's old tariff put breakfast at 25 cents. Lay out the morning: two notices for trades, a yard waiting on winter, and a wharf that never stops.
